Understanding breed predisposition to osteosarcoma and the growing need for canine oncology
Cancer is one of the leading causes of death in older dogs, yet many cancers remain difficult to diagnose and treat effectively.
ValiRx Animal Health
Company Update
October 30, 2026
Share
The statistics around osteosarcoma paint a stark picture: while thedisease remains relatively rare across the overall canine population, certainbreeds face a dramatically elevated risk. For companies like ValiRx AnimalHealth, these findings reinforce why advancing veterinary oncology is notsimply about treating disease when it occurs, but about improving earlierdiagnosis, expanding treatment options and ultimately enhancing quality of lifefor dogs and their owners.
The challenge
Cancer is one of the leading causes of death in older dogs, yetmany cancers remain difficult to diagnose and treat effectively. Osteosarcoma,an aggressive bone tumour associated with significant pain and reduced qualityof life, presents a particular challenge. While the condition affects only asmall proportion of the overall canine population, some breeds face anexceptionally high risk.
Analysis of more than 905,000 dogs within the VetCompass Programmeidentified 331 cases of osteosarcoma, representing an overall prevalence ofjust 0.037%. However, beneath this seemingly low figure lies a significantbreed-specific burden.
The evidence
The
study
into theprevalence of osteosarcoma in certain dog breeds revealed that several largeand giant breeds are disproportionately affected:
Scottish Deerhounds were found to be the most at-risk breed, with3.28% of dogs affected and a staggering 118-fold greater risk than crossbreddogs.
Leonbergers demonstrated a 1.48% prevalence and were nearly 56times more likely to develop osteosarcoma.
Great Danes showed a 34-fold increased risk, with 0.87% affected.
Rottweilers carried a 27-fold increased risk, with 0.84% affected.
Greyhounds were also among the most frequently affected breeds,with a prevalence of 0.62%.
The research further identified that heavier dogs, long-leggedbreeds and dogs with longer skull conformations were at greater risk, whileshorter-legged breeds appeared significantly protected.
Why does this matter?
For affected dogs, osteosarcoma is more than a diagnosis: it is apainful, progressive disease that can significantly impact mobility, wellbeingand longevity. For owners, the diagnosis often arrives suddenly and isaccompanied by difficult treatment decisions.
The findings highlight an important reality within veterinarymedicine: while canine cancer is often discussed as a broad category, there arespecific populations of dogs that face a markedly higher risk and would benefitfrom improved screening, monitoring and treatment pathways.
As dog ownership continues to evolve, with many owners viewing petsas integral family members, expectations around cancer care are alsoincreasing. Pet owners are seeking access to more sophisticated diagnostics,targeted therapies and treatment options that can help extend both lifespan andquality of life.
The opportunity for oncology innovation
The strong link between breed characteristics and osteosarcomademonstrates the value of precision approaches within veterinary oncology.Understanding which dogs are most at risk creates opportunities to supportearlier recognition of cancer symptoms, improve risk-based monitoring andveterinary decision-making, develop more targeted therapeutic strategies,generate data to support future oncology research all of which will provideowners with a deeper understanding and all them to make better-informed choicesaround treatment and care.
Importantly, osteosarcoma shares many biological and clinicalsimilarities with the human form of the disease. This creates a uniqueopportunity for comparative oncology, where advances in canine cancer researchcan contribute to broader scientific understanding and accelerate innovationacross both animal and human health.
ValiRx Animal Health perspective
At ValiRx Animal Health, we believe that improving outcomes forpets requires a greater focus on innovative oncology solutions. Studies such asthis demonstrate that canine cancer is not a niche concern but an area ofsignificant unmet need, particularly within breeds known to carry an elevatedrisk.
By supporting the development of next-generation cancerdiagnostics, therapeutics and research programmes, there is an opportunity tomove beyond symptom management towards more personalised and effectivetreatment strategies.
As our understanding of breed-specific cancer risk continues togrow, so too does the potential to transform how veterinary oncology ispractised, helping clinicians diagnose earlier, treat more effectively andultimately improve the lives of dogs living with cancer.
While osteosarcoma affects just 0.037% of the overall caninepopulation, some breeds are over 100 times more likely to develop the diseasethan crossbred dogs. These findings underline the urgent need for continuedinvestment in canine oncology research, earlier detection tools and innovativetreatments that can help improve outcomes for dogs most at risk.
